newsitem.title: USA: Former U.S. Supreme Court Justice Brennan dies.
newsitem.headline: Former U.S. Supreme Court Justice Brennan dies.

text.p: Former U.S. Supreme Court Justice William Brennan, whose landmark liberal rulings made him one of the most influential jurists in American history, died on Thursday.
Brennan, who retired in 1990 after serving 34 years on the nation's highest court, was 91. His precedent-setting rulings dramatically expanded the civil and constitutional rights of most Americans.
A Supreme Court spokesman said Brennan, who had been in failing health, died at 12:15 p.m. (1615 GMT) on Thursday after a long illness.
The spokesman said Brennan died at a nursing home in the nearby suburb of Arlington, Virginia, where Brennan had been undergoing rehabilitation for a broken hip suffered in November.

President Bill Clinton described Brennan as "one of the finest and most influential jurists in our nation's history," calling him "the staunchest, most effective defender of individual freedom against government intrusion."

In remarks during an unrelated White House event on global climate change, Clinton said, "His devotion to the Bill of Rights inspired millions of Americans and countless young law students, including myself."
He added, "The force of his ideas, the strength of his leadership and his character have safeguarded freedom and widened the circle of equality for every single one of us."

Chief Justice William Rehnquist, a conservative who often disagreed with the views of his former liberal colleague, praised Brennan. "He was a warm-hearted colleague to those of us who served with him," Rehnquist said in a statement.
"Justice Brennan served as member of the Supreme Court for more than a third of a century. During that time, he played a major role in shaping American constitutional law," Rehnquist said.

Attorney General Janet Reno said, "America has lost a great justice. Justice Brennan stood up for people who had no voice. He devoted his long, rich life to helping the American justice system live up to its ideals."
Brennan, whose tenure spanned those of eight presidents, wrote more than 1,200 opinions -- the second highest number in Supreme Court history.

Brennan was succeeded by Justice David Souter, who was supposed to be a conservative jurist. Instead, Souter, who has publicly expressed his admiration for Brennan, became one of the court's more liberal members.
